claims.text: Melt-spinning Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 at cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s produces an amorphous initial state.
The melt-spun amorphous alloy may contain nanoscale embryonic crystalline nuclei.
Flash annealing immediately after rapid quenching can increase amorphous retention in Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
Flash annealing immediately after rapid quenching can increase the thermal stability of amorphous Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20.
The proposed flash-annealing protocol uses a reheating rate above 10^3 K/s.
The proposed flash-annealing protocol heats the sample to approximately 0.9 times the crystallization-onset temperature and holds it for only a few milliseconds.
Flash annealing relaxes frozen-in structural heterogeneities and internal stresses in the amorphous matrix.
Flash annealing eradicates embryonic crystalline nuclei in the amorphous matrix.
Ultra-rapid sub-crystallization reheating permits stress-relieving atomic rearrangements without sufficient thermal exposure for full crystallization.
Removing misaligned short-range order and embryonic nuclei produces a more homogeneous amorphous matrix.
The flash-annealed alloy will exhibit a sharper, singular glass transition in DSC than untreated or conventionally reheated material.
The flash-annealed alloy will exhibit a higher crystallization-onset temperature than untreated or conventionally reheated material.
Flash annealing will significantly reduce the multistep crystallization exotherms observed by DSC.
The unmodified alloy exhibits extensive primary crystallization after rapid cooling and standard reheating.
Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 exhibits complex multiphase and multistep crystallization behavior.
Slow cooling of Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 produces multiple crystalline phases, whereas faster cooling reduces the number of phases and melt-spinning produces an amorphous structure.
The effective flash-annealing window is narrowly confined to temperatures just below the initial crystallization temperature and millisecond dwell times.
Temperatures or dwell times below the proposed window may produce incomplete structural relaxation.
A temperature overshoot or excessive dwell time may trigger crystallization.
The hypothesis is falsified if flash-annealed samples retain control-like multiple DSC exotherms, show significant crystalline phases by XRD, or have comparable embryonic-nucleus densities by TEM.
